title: Overview of Model Tax Conventions
outcomes: Compare the OECD, UN and US Models.
Apply persons covered and residence tie-breakers.
Apply PE and business profits rules.
Identify distributive rules for specific income.

meta.exam_tip: State which Model the clause follows before applying thresholds.

concepts.title: OECD, UN and US Models
body: The OECD Model began with a 1963 draft, was substantially revised in 1977 and is updated periodically (latest 2025). It favours residence-state taxation and is used mainly between developed countries.

The UN Model, finalised in 1980 and updated in 2001, 2011, 2017, 2021 and 2025, gives greater taxing rights to source (often developing) countries — for example, wider PE definitions, a service PE, and articles on fees for services and automated digital services. The US Model reflects US treaty policy.

Both Models have seven chapters (OECD 32 articles, UN 31) with broadly similar numbering (scope, definitions, taxation of income, methods for elimination of double taxation, special provisions); their Commentaries are key interpretive aids.
concepts.analogy: OECD leans to residence; UN protects source.
concepts.work: India's treaties often borrow UN-style service PE clauses.

concepts.title: Persons covered and residence
body: Article 1 covers persons resident of one or both states; provisions deal with fiscally transparent entities and a saving clause preserving a state's right to tax its own residents. The UN Model 2025 adds a rule requiring source-state relief only where the residence state actually taxes, to address double non-taxation.
Article 2 lists taxes covered (taxes on income and capital). Article 3 defines terms; undefined terms take domestic meaning unless context requires otherwise (Article 3(2)).

Article 4 defines a resident as a person liable to tax by reason of domicile, residence, place of management or similar criteria. Dual-resident individuals are resolved by tie-breakers in order: permanent home, centre of vital interests, habitual abode, nationality, and finally mutual agreement. For non-individuals, the current Models leave residence to competent authorities by mutual agreement.
concepts.analogy: Residence decides treaty access; tie-breakers decide which state.
concepts.work: Family ties abroad can make an Indian dual resident a resident of the other state.

concepts.title: Permanent establishment and business profits
body: Article 5 defines a permanent establishment: a fixed place of business (office, branch, factory, mine), construction sites lasting over 12 months (OECD) or over 6 months (UN), and dependent agents who habitually conclude or play the principal role in concluding contracts. Preparatory or auxiliary activities are excluded, subject to anti-fragmentation rules.

The UN Model adds a service PE where services are furnished through employees for more than 183 days in any twelve-month period, and includes agents maintaining stock for delivery; the insurance PE clause was removed in 2025 in favour of a separate insurance premiums article.

Article 7 allows the source state to tax business profits only if attributable to a PE; the UN Model contains a limited force-of-attraction rule covering sales and activities similar to those through the PE.
concepts.analogy: No PE, no source tax on business profits.
concepts.work: An 8-month construction project is a PE under the UN Model but not the OECD Model.

concepts.title: Distributive rules for specific income
body: Article 8 gives international shipping and air transport profits to the residence state (with UN alternatives for shipping). Articles 10, 11 and 12 allow source taxation of dividends, interest and royalties at capped rates (OECD gives royalties exclusively to residence).

UN-specific articles: 12AA (fees for services, replacing the former 12A on technical services and Article 14 in 2025), 12B (income from automated digital services, added in 2021, taxable on a gross or net basis at the taxpayer's option), and 12C (insurance premiums).

Article 13 covers capital gains, including gains from shares deriving value from immovable property (tested over 365 days). Articles 15 to 21 cover employment, directors' fees, entertainers and sportspersons, pensions, government service, students and other income; Articles 23–27 deal with elimination of double taxation, non-discrimination, MAP, exchange of information and assistance in collection.
concepts.analogy: Distributive rules allocate each income type.
concepts.work: Fees for services from India to a UN-model treaty partner may be taxed in India under Article 12AA.

illustrations.title: PE under OECD and UN Models
illustrations.q: (a) A foreign contractor runs a construction project in India lasting 8 months. (b) A foreign consultancy sends staff who are present in India for 45, 60, 50 and 45 days across four visits within a twelve-month period (no fixed place used). Does a PE arise under the OECD and UN Models?

OECD Model
UN Model
rows: 8 months — not above 12 months: no PE
No service PE article: test fixed place
200 days exceed 183 in 12 months: service PE

viva.q: Why does the UN Model widen the PE definition?
viva.model: To preserve taxing rights of source countries, typically developing countries.

viva.q: How is dual residence of a company resolved under current Models?
viva.model: By mutual agreement between competent authorities, considering place of effective management and other factors.

viva.q: What is a dependent agent PE?
viva.model: An agent who habitually concludes contracts or plays the principal role in concluding them for the enterprise.

viva.q: How may Article 12B income be taxed?
viva.model: On a gross basis at a capped rate, or on a net basis at the taxpayer's option.
Undefined terms take their domestic-law meaning unless the context requires otherwise.
